title: Security Controls: Org Policy, Hierarchical Firewall, VPC-SC, Context-Aware Access, and Auditing
bodyMarkdown:
## Preventive, detective, and perimeter controls

Strong designs layer **preventive** controls (the bad thing cannot happen), **perimeter** controls (valid credentials still cannot cross a boundary), and **detective** controls (you find out quickly and can prove what happened). This module maps each requirement to the control that actually satisfies it, which is the skill the exam tests.

| Requirement phrase | Control |
|---|---|
| "No VM may ever have an external IP, owners cannot override" | Organization Policy constraint at the org node |
| "Consistent baseline firewall rules app teams cannot weaken" | Hierarchical firewall policy |
| "Stolen credentials must not copy data to an outside project" | VPC Service Controls perimeter |
| "Employees reach internal apps from anywhere, only from healthy devices, no VPN" | IAP + Chrome Enterprise Premium access levels |
| "Tamper-evident history of IAM changes, retained for years" | Admin Activity logs + org-level aggregated sink |
| "One view of misconfigurations and threats" | Security Command Center |

## Organization Policy constraints

Constraints restrict **how resources may be configured**, inherit down the hierarchy, and are administered separately from workload ownership. The [constraint reference](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/org-policy-constraints) documents the ones the exam keeps returning to:

- `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess`: controls whether VMs may use IPv4 external addresses. By default **all VMs are allowed** external IPs, so you must set it to deny-all at the org node to get the guarantee.
- `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`: blocks service account key creation when enforced.
- `constraints/compute.requireOsLogin`: enables OS Login on all newly created projects.
- `constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess`: disables serial port access for the scope where it is enforced.
- `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations`: limits where new resources are created.

The [defining locations documentation](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/defining-locations) contains important caveats. `gcp.resourceLocations` applies only to **newly created** resources, does not affect global resources, covers only a subset of services, can take up to **15 minutes** to take effect, and is explicitly **not a data residency commitment**: it does not guarantee where data is stored. It accepts value groups such as `in:eu-locations` that expand automatically as locations are added. That is why regulated designs pair it with Assured Workloads (module 5) instead of using it alone.

Remember the lifecycle features from module 1: dry-run mode to see violations before enforcing, no retroactive effect on existing resources, and tag-based conditional enforcement.

## Hierarchical firewall policies

A hierarchical firewall policy is associated with an **organization or folder**, so it applies across many VPC networks and projects. Per the [firewall policies overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-overview), rules allow or deny traffic and can use **secure tags**, **FQDN objects**, **geolocation objects**, and address groups, which classic VPC firewall rules do not offer. Hierarchical policy rules are evaluated first; regional system firewall policy rules are evaluated immediately after them, and only then the VPC-level policy and rules your app teams own.

The design pattern is a **non-overridable baseline** at the org or folder: allow the IAP TCP-forwarding range for SSH and RDP, deny everything else inbound by default, and let teams add their own VPC rules for application traffic. Use a hierarchical policy rather than copying the same rule into every project's VPC; the latter drifts and can be edited by project owners.

## VPC Service Controls

VPC Service Controls creates a **service perimeter** around Google Cloud resources. The [overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview) describes the default behavior: free communication inside the perimeter, and **blocked communication to protected Google Cloud services across the perimeter**. It mitigates exfiltration through stolen OAuth or service account credentials, malicious insiders or compromised code, and mistakes in IAM, because the check is **independent of IAM**. It complements IAM and never replaces it.

Mechanics to know:

- **Ingress rules** let clients outside the perimeter reach resources inside; **egress rules** let clients or resources inside reach resources outside. The [ingress and egress rules documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/ingress-egress-rules) shows both use a `from` block (identities and sources) and a `to` block (services, methods, resources). Identity choices include `ANY_IDENTITY`, `ANY_USER_ACCOUNT`, `ANY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, or specific principals; ingress sources can be access levels, projects, folders, organizations, VPC networks, or Private Service Connect endpoints. Resources are referenced by project, folder, or organization number.
- **Access levels** (from Access Context Manager) classify requests by attributes such as source IP range, device, and geolocation, and can be attached to a perimeter so only matching contexts get in.
- **Dry-run mode** logs what would be blocked without blocking, which is the safe way to find the rules you need before enforcing.
- **Perimeter bridges** still exist, but ingress and egress rules are now recommended for granular control.
- **Do not add unsupported services** to a perimeter; the documentation warns this causes unexpected issues.

| Question | IAM | VPC-SC |
|---|---|---|
| Is this identity allowed to call this API? | Yes | No |
| Is this request coming from inside an approved boundary? | No | Yes |
| Does it stop a valid stolen credential from copying data to an attacker's project? | No | Yes |
| Can it replace IAM? | n/a | No |

## Context-aware access

For users, the [Chrome Enterprise Premium overview](https://cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise-premium/docs/overview) (the product formerly branded BeyondCorp Enterprise) enforces decisions based on identity, device security posture, and location, using access levels from Access Context Manager. It supports **VPN-less access** to a web application on Google Cloud or elsewhere, and integrates device signals from third-party vendors. [Identity-Aware Proxy](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview) is the enforcement point in front of the app: it authenticates the user and checks IAM before granting access, and the documentation stresses that you must also block traffic that bypasses it (firewall rules for VMs, ingress controls or disabling the `run.app` URL for Cloud Run).

### Chrome Enterprise Premium in practice

The [access protection overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise-premium/docs/access-protection) describes a zero-trust model: no access unless every rule is met, with IAP as the enforcement layer, **Access Context Manager** as the rules engine (IP subnetworks, regions, principals, device policy), **Endpoint Verification** (a Chrome extension reporting device encryption status and OS), and **IAM Conditions** tying them together. It replaces per-user VPN access to apps.

Mechanics from the [access levels guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise-premium/docs/access-levels):

- An access level is enforced as an **IAM condition on the IAP role** (`roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor`) bound to the user or group. Until it is bound there, it does nothing.
- Several levels on one binding are **OR**ed; to require all of them, combine them into a single level.
- Device-based conditions work only after Endpoint Verification is deployed.
- URL-path conditions require exact matching and can be bypassed by encoded variants, so never make a path condition your only barrier.

**Certificate-based access** goes further: per the [CBA documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise-premium/docs/cba-endpoint-verification-certs), device certificates enforce every request through an mTLS handshake rather than a periodic check. It can protect the Cloud console, APIs and storage, with full support on macOS and Windows (Chrome) and macOS, Windows and Linux (Google Cloud CLI).

Per the [product overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise-premium/docs/overview), Chrome Enterprise Premium also adds in-browser **threat and data protection** (malware sandboxing, phishing protection, DLP controls over copy, paste, download and print), protects apps on Google Cloud, other clouds, on-premises and SaaS, and needs a **separate license** beyond free Chrome Enterprise Core. **Choose it for user-to-app access** that depends on identity and device posture. **Choose VPC Service Controls** for the API-to-data perimeter. They answer different questions and are often combined.

## Auditing and Security Command Center

The [Cloud Audit Logs documentation](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) defines four log types:

| Log type | Captures | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Admin Activity** | API calls that modify configuration or metadata, including IAM policy changes | Always on, cannot be disabled; stored in `_Required` |
| **Data Access** | API calls that read configuration or user data | Off by default except BigQuery; enable explicitly; stored in `_Default` |
| **System Event** | Google-initiated changes such as autoscaling | Always on; `_Required` |
| **Policy Denied** | Access denied because of a security policy violation | Generated by default, cannot be disabled, storage can be excluded |

Entries written by Cloud Audit Logs are **immutable**. Data Access logs can raise cost, so enable them for sensitive datasets (PHI, PII, secrets) rather than blindly everywhere. Viewing Data Access logs requires the Private Logs Viewer role.

**Google personnel access.** Cloud Audit Logs record what *your* principals did; **Access Transparency** logs record what *Google personnel* did to your Customer Data, including the resource, action, time, justification reason and accessor details such as location, employing entity and job category ([overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/access-transparency/docs/overview)). **Access Approval** goes further: Customer Care and engineering must obtain your **explicit approval** before access, via email or Pub/Sub notification. Each request is cryptographically signed (Google-managed key by default, or your own Cloud KMS or Cloud EKM key), and you can revoke an active approval at any time ([overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/access-approval/docs/overview)). Transparency is detective; approval is preventive. The trade-off: **support response time grows by the time spent waiting for your approval**, so be cautious enabling it for services needing rapid support. Inside an Assured Workloads boundary, the personnel assurances apply before Access Approval is evaluated. By default it enrolls all supported services.

For long retention and org-wide visibility, use an **aggregated sink** at the organization node. The [aggregated sinks documentation](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks) describes `includeChildren` to collect from every child resource, destinations of a log bucket, BigQuery dataset, Cloud Storage bucket, or Pub/Sub topic, and the sink's service account needing the matching writer role at the destination (for example `roles/logging.bucketWriter` or `roles/bigquery.dataEditor`). Route to a **dedicated, access-restricted** destination so the people being audited cannot alter or read their own trail. Up to 50 exclusion filters per sink let you control volume.

**Security Command Center** ([overview](https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/security-command-center-overview)) is the detective layer: misconfigurations, exposed resources, leaked credentials, threat detection (Event Threat Detection, Container Threat Detection, VM Threat Detection), compliance posture against frameworks such as NIST, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS, and attack-path simulation. It can be activated at project or organization level. The overview page lists the Enterprise tier as deprecated with a shutdown date of May 21, 2027, so verify current tier availability before recommending it.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Relying on IAM alone to prevent exfiltration.** A valid token still works from anywhere without VPC-SC.
- **Using `gcp.resourceLocations` as a residency guarantee.** It only restricts new resource locations for supported services.
- **Copy-pasting firewall rules per project** instead of using a hierarchical policy.
- **Enforcing a perimeter without dry-run**, then breaking pipelines that legitimately call across it.
- **Enabling Data Access logs everywhere** and then excluding them under cost pressure, leaving gaps where PHI lives.
- **Sending audit logs to a destination the audited team administers.**
- **Placing IAP in front of an app but leaving a direct public path**, which bypasses it.
- **Applying an access level without binding it to the IAP role**, or expecting two levels on one binding to combine as AND.
- **Turning on Access Approval for a latency-sensitive production service** with no one on call to approve.
- **Expecting an Organization Policy to fix existing violations**; it is not retroactive.

## Exam tips

- **"Cannot be overridden by a project owner":** Organization Policy at the org node (for external IPs, `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` set to deny); the default allows external IPs.
- **Baseline firewall above project level:** hierarchical firewall policy on the org or folder, evaluated before VPC rules.
- **Exfiltration with valid credentials:** VPC Service Controls perimeter; refine with ingress/egress rules and access levels, test in dry-run first.
- **VPC-SC is not IAM:** it complements roles and never replaces them.
- **VPN-less, device-aware access:** IAP plus Chrome Enterprise Premium access levels from Access Context Manager based on device posture.
- **Access levels do nothing until bound:** attach them as an IAM condition on the IAP accessor role; multiple levels are OR, a single combined level is AND; device posture needs Endpoint Verification.
- **Google staff access:** Access Transparency logs it (detective), Access Approval gates it (preventive) at the cost of slower support.
- **IAM change history:** Admin Activity logs are always on; add an org-level aggregated sink to a restricted BigQuery dataset or bucket for retention and query.
- **Data Access logs are off by default** (except BigQuery); turn them on for PHI and PII.
- **Residency:** `gcp.resourceLocations` limits new resource locations only; pair with Assured Workloads when personnel and support access matter.
